food.text: By the early 16th century, coffee drinking had spread from Yemen and Arabia to reach Damascus, Cairo and Istanbul. It soon became a central part of urban social life across these Ottoman cities.

In the 16th century, Hebron's charitable 'Table of Abraham' (simat al-Khalil), reinstated by the Mamluk sultan Qaytbay in the 15th century, was still giving free lentils to travelers every day. According to the chronicler Mujir al-Din, all visitors were welcome at this table.

Ottoman trade routes carried new ingredients from Asia and the Americas into Levantine kitchens, enriching the region's cuisine. The historian Fernand Braudel credits the Ottomans with introducing rice, sesame and maize to the region.

In 1524, Ottoman Sultan Suleiman I overturned earlier bans on coffee after Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-Imadi issued a fatwa permitting its consumption. This cleared the way for coffee culture to flourish in cities such as Damascus, which had become part of the Ottoman Empire's coffee-drinking world by the early 16th century.

On Thursday evenings, Hebron's Table of Abraham departed from its usual lentil fare to serve pomegranate seeds and seasoned rice known as ruzz mufalfal. This weekly variation was part of the same charitable tradition that fed travelers in the city throughout the 16th century.

Between 1507 and 1515, the Portuguese commander Albuquerque tried to cut off traditional Arab spice trade routes running from western India to the Mediterranean. He did this by seizing strategic bases in the Persian Gulf and at the entrance to the Red Sea.

Writing in the 17th century, the Ottoman traveler Evliya Celebi described receiving a bowl of wheat soup at Hebron's Table of Abraham, calling it a gift from God. He said he had never tasted such a good meal, even at the tables of viziers or scholars.

art.text: By 1590, Baghdad had re-emerged as a flourishing center of illustrated book production, a role it had lost after the Mongols sacked the city. This revival launched a new era of manuscript painting in Mesopotamia at the close of the 16th century.

Damascus remained a center of innovative pottery production in the Islamic world until around 1600, continuing a tradition of craftsmanship that had begun there around 1100. It outlasted other renowned centers such as Tabriz, whose production ended by 1550.

In Aleppo, a wealthy Christian broker's reception hall was lined with painted wooden panels, now known as the Aleppo Room. Inscriptions date them to 1600–01 or 1603, which makes them the oldest Syrian art of this kind that still exists.

Al-Azm Palace in Damascus was built in 1749 as the private residence of As'ad Pasha al-Azm, the city's governor. It rose over the site of a former Mamluk palace and was built by 800 workers over three years. A local barber, Shaikh Ahmad Al-Bidiri Al-Halaq, recorded in his diary that whenever al-Azm heard of an antiquity or rare work of marble or porcelain, he would send someone to get it, "with or without the owner's consent".

Ahmad Pasha el-Jazzar ordered the el-Jazzar Mosque in Acre in 1781 and had it finished within the year. He had no architectural training, yet he drew up the plans and design himself and supervised the whole construction. He modeled it on the mosques of Istanbul.

The Baghdad school of painting that flourished from 1590 placed a stronger focus on everyday activities than miniature painting produced elsewhere in the Ottoman world at the time. This distinguished Baghdad's revived manuscripts from those made in other centers.

Most Islamic decoration is dominated by plant motifs, but the Aleppo Room panels also show scenes with people and with animals. A Persian artist carved them in 1603. They include painted Christian scenes of the Virgin Mary, Christ and his disciples.

Al-Azm Palace covers 6400 square metres and is an example of traditional Damascene houses. It has three wings: the harem for the family, the selamlek for guests, and the khademlek. The family baths are a smaller replica of the city's public hammams.

The el-Jazzar Mosque was built over earlier Muslim and Christian prayer houses and Crusader buildings. Its marble and granite came from the ancient ruins of Caesarea, Atlit and medieval Acre. Greek masons were commissioned as the builders.

The Aleppo Room was made for a Christian citizen of the Ottoman Empire at the beginning of the 17th century. In this reception hall, in the Al-Jdayde quarter, he welcomed visitors from other ethnic and religious backgrounds.
The builders of Al-Azm Palace used limestone, sandstone, basalt and marble so the walls would have varied decoration. The ceilings have painted wooden panels showing natural scenes.

The el-Jazzar Mosque was first named Masjid al-Anwar, the "Great Mosque of Lights". It is also called the White Mosque because its silvery-white dome once glittered from far away. The dome is now painted green, and the minaret has a winding staircase of 124 steps.
Beit Ghazaleh in Aleppo is a 17th-century mansion known for its fine decorations. The Armenian sculptor Khachadur Bali carved them in 1691.

After the Muslim conquest of Acre, the Franciscans fled the city. They returned in 1620 to establish the Terra Sancta Church, the only church in the eastern Old City. Saint George Greek Orthodox Cathedral was built before 1631 and is considered the oldest Christian church in Acre. The Franciscan Saint John the Baptist Church followed in 1737, under Ottoman rule.

At the entrance of the el-Jazzar Mosque, six poetic verses were engraved in blue marble, and for a long time locals puzzled over their meaning. The poem was written by the judge Yusuf bin Ahmad al-Rimawi al-Hashemi for his son Ahmed, urging him to go early to the mosque and take up his position as judge. It also praises the builder, Ahmad, as a bold statesman who became "The butcher of the necks of enemies as deserved."

war.text: The Ottoman–Safavid War of 1623–1639 was fought between the Ottoman Empire and Safavid Iran, then the two major powers of Western Asia. The prize was control of Mesopotamia. The war ended with the Treaty of Zuhab, an Ottoman victory.

The Safavids began the war with success, taking Baghdad on 14 January 1624 and then most of Ottoman Iraq, which they had lost for 90 years. The fall of Baghdad was followed by the massacre of a large part of its Sunni inhabitants, as the Shah endeavored to transform it into a purely Shiite city. The war then became a stalemate, as the Safavids could not press further and the Ottomans were distracted by wars in Europe and weakened by internal turmoil. The Ottomans finally recovered Baghdad, but took heavy losses in the final siege.

The Treaty of Zuhab roughly restored the borders of 1555. The Safavids kept Daghestan, Shirvan, eastern Georgia and Eastern Armenia, while western Georgia and Western Armenia came under Ottoman rule. Mesopotamia stayed in Ottoman hands until the aftermath of World War I.

In 1624, the Turkish pasha of Basra was being pressed by a Safavid army led by Imam Quli Khan. He made an alliance with the Portuguese. The Ottoman-Portuguese coalition inflicted a severe defeat on the Persians, who retreated from Basra.
The Ottoman Turks took Baghdad from the Persians in 1535. This established Ottoman rule in Iraq and gave the empire naval access to the Persian Gulf.

Having vanquished the Safavid Persians at Chaldiran in 1514, Sultan Selim I turned on the Mamluk Sultanate in 1516. Both sides fielded 60,000 soldiers, but only 15,000 of the Mamluks were trained warriors; the rest were conscripts who did not even know how to fire a musket, and most of them fled, avoided the front lines, or even committed suicide. The blasts of Ottoman cannons and guns also scared the Mamluk horses, which raced uncontrollably in every direction, as had happened to the Safavids at Chaldiran.

Hüsrev Pasha besieged Baghdad in November, but had to lift the siege soon after because another heavy winter threatened his lines of communication. After he withdrew, the Persians re-established their control of Iraq and subdued the rebellious Kurdish populations.

Ottoman control of Mesopotamia after 1639 was not entirely unbroken. Iranians briefly retook parts of it during the reigns of Nader Shah (1736–1747) and Karim Khan Zand (1751–1779). It nevertheless remained in Ottoman hands until the aftermath of World War I.

During the long stalemate, after years of constant raiding and skirmishes with neither side gaining a decisive advantage, Shah Safi sent a peace delegation to the Ottoman court, but the new Grand Vizier, Tabanıyassi Mehmed Pasha, rejected its demands.

literature.text: Fuzuli, a 16th-century poet born in what is now Iraq, became one of the greatest poets of Turkic literature by composing in Azerbaijani, Persian, and Arabic. His fame reached from Central Asia to India between the 16th and 19th centuries.

The Ottoman traveler Evliya Çelebi visited Palestine twice, once in 1649 and once in 1670 to 1671. He recorded these and other journeys, spanning more than 40 years, in a ten-volume travelogue called the Seyahatname.

Isaac Luria was a Jewish mystic who settled in Safed around 1570 and came to be considered the father of contemporary Kabbalah, even though he personally wrote only a few poems. His authority was so respected that his disciples scrutinized his every custom, and many were adopted even against earlier practice.

Fuzuli lived in Iraq as it passed between three empires, the Aq Qoyunlu, the Safavid, and the Ottoman, and he composed poetry for officials of all three. He dedicated his first known poem to Shah Alvand Mirza of the Aq Qoyunlu.

Fuzuli's retelling of the story of Leylī and Macnūn was praised by the Encyclopaedia Iranica for raising the tragedy to a plane of mystical longing. It became known as one of the greatest works of Turkic literature.

Unlike most European and some Jewish travelogues of Palestine and Syria in the 17th century, Evliya Çelebi wrote one of the few detailed accounts from an Islamic point of view. He noted, "All chronicles call this country Palestine."

Ottoman scholar Kâtip Çelebi's love of collecting books began in Aleppo, where his army corps wintered in 1633 before he set out on the Hajj. He later spent much of his inheritance building a personal library that became the largest in Istanbul.

Luria delivered his mystical teachings almost entirely through spoken lectures, with only a few poems ever written down. His disciple Vital collected these lecture notes into written works, the most important being the eight-volume Etz Chaim, or 'Tree of Life.'

Kurdish literature has its earliest works in the 16th-century poet Malaye Jaziri of western Kurdistan. Gurani, the language of the Guran Kurds in Hawraman, also produced a literary tradition originating from the 16th century. It includes the religious texts of Yarsanism.

After Fuzuli's patron Ibrahim Khan Mawsillu was murdered by his own nephew in 1527, the poet moved to Hilla or Najaf. There he worked as custodian of the Imam Ali Shrine, though he still had little money.
Despite wishing to see far-off places like Tabriz, Anatolia, and India, Fuzuli never traveled outside Iraq during his life. He died of the plague in 1556 and was buried in Karbala.

One volume of Evliya Çelebi's Seyahatname follows his pilgrimage route through southern Anatolia, Syria, Aleppo, and Damascus on the way to Medina and Mecca. The same route also passed through Smyrna, Ephesus, Rhodes, and Suez.

Luria's disciples swore, on pain of excommunication, not to let copies of his teachings leave Ottoman Syria, so for years the manuscripts of the Etz Chaim stayed there. Eventually one copy reached Europe and was published at Zolkiev in 1772 by Isaac Satanow.

politics.text: In 1516, after the Ottomans conquered Egypt and Syria, areas inhabited by the Maronites became part of the Tripoli Eyalet, placed under the authority of the governor of Damascus. Seeking a protective power in Europe, the Maronites later gained France as their official protector in 1649.

Under Fakhr-al-Din II, Druze rule expanded to cover Lebanon-Phoenicia and much of Syria, stretching from the Antioch plain in the north to Safad in the south, and including his castle at Tadmur, the site of ancient Palmyra. His growing strength eventually made him too powerful for his Ottoman sovereign in Constantinople.

On 24 August 1516, the Ottomans defeated the Mamluk Sultanate at the Battle of Marj Dabiq, near Aleppo. The Mamluks had at first killed several thousand Turkish soldiers, but the sultan al-Ghawri died on the field and his army collapsed. The victory gave Selim's armies control of the entire region of Syria and opened the door to the conquest of Egypt.

Fakhr al-Din II, a Druze emir of Mount Lebanon, ruled much of the Levant from the 1620s to 1633. He united Lebanon's Druze and Maronites under a single authority and is generally regarded as the country's founder. Though he ruled in the Ottomans' name, he acted with considerable autonomy and cultivated ties with European powers.

The Ottoman–Safavid War of 1623–1639 was fought over Mesopotamia. The Safavids took Baghdad on 14 January 1624, with the aid of Bakr's son, Muhammad, having lost it for 90 years, and the fall of the city was followed by the massacre of a large part of its Sunni inhabitants, as the Shah endeavored to transform Baghdad into a purely Shiite city. The Ottomans retook it in December 1638 under Murad IV after a siege of 39 days, taking heavy losses in the final siege. The Treaty of Zuhab, concluded on 17 May 1639, ended the war in an Ottoman victory.

In 1608 Fakhr-al-Din II went so far as to sign a commercial treaty with Duke Ferdinand I of Tuscany containing secret military clauses. When the Ottoman Sultan sent a force against him, he was compelled to flee, seeking refuge at the courts of Tuscany in 1613 and Naples in 1615.

After defeating the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq, Selim I conquered Syria in 1516 and took Egypt in 1517 after the Battle of Ridanieh, ending the Mamluk Sultanate. Returning from Egypt in July 1517, he reorganized Syria into one large province called Şam, split into several districts or sanjaks.

In 1613 an imperial campaign was launched against Fakhr al-Din II for allying with Tuscany and garrisoning strategic fortresses. Ottoman forces blocked the roads and blockaded the port of Sidon, and he escaped only by bribing the deputy admiral of the blockade and boarding a European ship. While he was gone, Yusuf Sayfa's son Husayn burned Deir al-Qamar, the Ma'ns' headquarters village, until Ahmed Pasha ordered him to stop. Fakhr al-Din II lived in exile in Tuscany and Sicily and returned in 1618.

The Maan and Shihab government of Mount Lebanon between 1667 and 1841 was an Ottoman tax farm, not a dynastic principality. Their position was so precarious that in over three centuries only two significantly strong leaders emerged: Fakhr al-Din II and Bashir Shihab II.

Signed on 17 May 1639, the Treaty of Zuhab ceded all of Mesopotamia, including Baghdad, to the Ottomans, forming Ottoman Iraq. It ended almost 150 years of intermittent wars between the two empires and was seen as a confirmation of the earlier Peace of Amasya of 1555.

After the death of Mulhim, his sons Ahmad and Korkmaz fought a power struggle with other Ottoman-backed Druze leaders. Korkmaz was killed in an act of treachery by the Beylerbey of Damascus in 1662. Ahmad Ma'n emerged victorious in 1667 but lost control of Safad, retreating to rule the Shuf mountains and Kisrawan until his death from natural causes, without an heir, in 1697. During the Ottoman–Habsburg War (1683–1699) he had joined a rebellion against the Ottomans that continued even after his death.

Before marching, Selim I sent an embassy offering friendly terms. He promised to agree to Mamluk requests to appoint an Egyptian vassal to the Beylik of Dulkadir, a longstanding buffer state between the two powers, and to reopen the frontier to trade in goods and slaves. It was a ruse: when a second embassy arrived with lavish presents and the Mamluk chancellor Mughla Bey was sent back with counter-gifts, Selim had dropped the pretense of peace. The Ottomans scorned the embassy and returned him with his head and beard shaved, riding a lame mount.

Ottoman rule in Syria kept being redrawn. Aleppo was split into its own eyalet in 1534, Tripoli was carved out of Damascus in 1579, and the Eyalet of Safed was created in 1660 and soon renamed Sidon. In 1667 the Mount Lebanon Emirate received a special autonomous status within Sidon province.

Ottoman wars against Safavid Iran and Habsburg Austria gave Fakhr al-Din II room to build his semi-autonomous power. Government records show his tax farms growing between 1591 and 1594 to include the Chouf, Matn, and the southern Beqaa Valley, plus salt profits from the ports of Acre, Sidon, and Beirut.

After Ahmad Ma'n died without an heir in 1697, the iltizam rights over the Shuf and Kisrawan passed to the rising Shihab family through female-line inheritance. This ended the Ma'ni dynasty's long hold on Druze leadership in the region.

Fakhr al-Din II used marriage as politics. After peace settlements with the rival Sayfa family, he wed Alwa, a daughter of Ali Sayfa, in 1613. His son Ali was married to Yusuf Sayfa's daughter in 1620, and a daughter of his was married to Yusuf's son Beylik the same year.

philosophy.text: Isaac Luria, known as Ha'ari, was a leading rabbi and Jewish mystic active in Safed, in the Galilee region of Ottoman Palestine, until his death in 1572. He is considered the father of contemporary Kabbalah, and his oral teachings became known as Lurianic Kabbalah.

In 1666, the Ottoman rabbi Sabbatai Zevi was proclaimed the Jewish Messiah by Nathan of Gaza, sparking a movement known as the Sabbateans. In February he was imprisoned in Constantinople. In September the grand vizier, in the name of Sultan Mehmed IV, gave him the choice of facing death by some type of ordeal or converting to Islam, and he seems to have chosen conversion. Vast numbers of Jews in the diaspora still accepted his claims.

Luria settled in Safed in 1570, after his teacher Moses Cordovero, who had led Kabbalistic studies there for decades, died that June. Luria then took over Cordovero's role as the community's foremost teacher of Kabbalah.

Luria never wrote down his teachings, aside from a few kabbalistic poems; instead his disciple Hayyim Vital collected the notes taken by students during his lectures. The most important resulting work, the eight-volume Etz Chaim, or Tree of Life, first circulated only in manuscript.
After Luria's death in Safed on July 25, 1572, he was buried in the town's old Jewish cemetery. The Ari Ashkenazi Synagogue in Safed was built in his memory later in the 16th century.

Lurianic Kabbalah taught new doctrines about the origins of Creation, describing two spiritual states called Olam HaTohu, the World of Tohu-Chaos, and Olam HaTikun, the World of Tikun-Rectification. These ideas grew out of Isaac Luria's own interpretation of the earlier Zohar.

Rabbi Hayyim ben Joseph Vital of Calabria was the main popularizer of Luria's ideas, claiming to be the official interpreter of the Lurianic system. The compiled teachings of Luria's school are together known as Kitvei HaARI, the Writings of the ARI.

Luria's disciples had to pledge, under threat of excommunication, not to let copies of his teachings leave Ottoman Syria. For a time every manuscript stayed there, until one finally reached Europe and was printed at Zolkiev in 1772.

Some scholars have blamed Lurianic Kabbalah for helping spread the Sabbatean movement of Shabbetai Tzvi, who lived from 1626 to 1676, and later that of Jacob Frank. This mystical revival began in 16th century Safed under teachers such as Moses Cordovero and Isaac Luria.

culture.text: In 1666 the Ottoman Jewish rabbi and Kabbalist Sabbatai Zevi (1626–1676) was proclaimed the Jewish Messiah by Nathan of Gaza, and vast numbers of Jews across the diaspora accepted his claim. Imprisoned in Constantinople that February, he was given the choice that September of facing death by some type of ordeal or converting to Islam, and he seems to have chosen conversion. Jewish communities were left horrified and disheartened, and Muslims and Christians jeered at the Jews, yet many of his followers, called Sabbateans, kept believing in him.

During the papacy of Pope Gregory XIII (1572–1585), the Maronites were drawn closer to Rome, and in 1584 he founded the Pontifical Maronite College there. This was one of the steps that strengthened ties between the Maronite Church and the Catholic Church.

The Lebanese Council of 1736 marked a major turning point for the Maronite Church, drawing it closer to the Latin Church. It was the only major Maronite council in modern times to set out detailed rules and canons for the community.

In the late seventeenth century, groups of Sabbatean believers from Poland migrated to Palestine, carrying the messianic movement into the Levant. Around the same time, a radical faction of the Dönmeh movement, led by Baruchiah Russo, emerged seeking to abolish many biblical prohibitions.

Jacob ben Aaron Sasportas (1610–1698) was among the fiercest opponents of the Sabbatean movement, writing letters to Jewish communities across Europe, Asia and Africa urging them to expose Sabbatai Zevi and his followers as impostors. He recorded his campaign against the movement in a book called Tzitzat Novel Tzvi.

Jacob Hagis (1620–1674), one of Sabbatai Zevi's chief opponents, placed him under a religious ban. Around 1673 Hagis traveled to Constantinople to publish his book Lehem ha-Panim, but he died there before it could be completed and the work was lost.
